overview: Totonac histories belong to the varied coastal and mountain landscapes of Veracruz and Puebla. Cities and communities shared some practices with neighbours while retaining local differences. Cempoala provides a documented example of urban life, rather than a model for every Totonac settlement.

periods.title: Regional life under Mexica pressure
periods.summary: Mexica expansion altered relations in Totonacapan. The region remained culturally diverse, with different settlements and languages rather than one uniform population.

periods.title: An alliance and a new conquest
periods.summary: Cempoala’s ruler allied with Cortés against Tenochtitlan. Totonac participation served local political aims, but Spanish domination brought new demands.

periods.title: Recognition of living traditions
periods.summary: International safeguarding recognised the Voladores ceremony and the Centre for Indigenous Arts. These dates concern recognition of continuing practices, not their invention.

items.text: Cempoala’s production areas lay both within and beyond its dispersed urban settlement. Cultivation and residence were interwoven, so the city should not be imagined as a compact block of buildings surrounded by all of its fields.

INAH describes walls protecting Cempoala against floods, channels bringing river water into the city and drains carrying wastewater toward cultivation. Managing water involved supply, protection and disposal together.

Cempoala’s temples included square and circular foundations. The circular building associated with Ehecatl contrasts with the square-based Quetzalcoatl temple, showing variation within one ceremonial centre.

At Yohualichan, INAH interprets architectural niches as references to caves in the surrounding region. Niches also appear at other sites, including El Tajín. Shared forms reveal connections, but alone cannot demonstrate that all such places belonged to one political state.

INPI’s account of later Totonac cuisine describes maize, beans and many edible greens, along with foods such as bocoles and handmade tortillas. This is evidence of a living regional cuisine; its complete modern ingredient list should not be projected into preconquest kitchens.

Backstrap weaving produces garments and household cloths. INPI describes Papantla makers using cotton or acrylic thread for a raised, soft-textured finish called confitillo. The presence of newer fibres shows a craft tradition adapting its materials.

In the Voladores ceremony, four performers descend on ropes from a tall pole while the caporal plays a flute and small drum above them. The coordinated movement, music and height make the ceremony a demanding collective performance.

UNESCO describes the ceremony as expressing relationships with nature and spiritual powers, including the sun and winds. It is especially associated with Totonac communities but also practised by other peoples. One community’s version should not stand for every performance.

The Centre for Indigenous Arts organises learning through houses devoted to pottery, textiles, music, cuisine and other arts. Elders teach values alongside technique. Totonac language is a medium of instruction, making cultural transmission part of everyday educational practice.

The centre’s safeguarding work includes recovering techniques and restoring plants and trees needed for artistic practice. This links the future of crafts with their material environments, as well as with the teachers and apprentices who keep knowledge in use.

ending.text: Alliance against the Mexica did not preserve independence from Spain. Colonial rule imposed labour and religious demands and later reorganised local authorities. Totonac communities continued, adapting institutions and maintaining languages and creative traditions; no single city’s decline ends their history.
